company.name: Basecamp (made by 37signals)
company.what_they_do: Basecamp is web-based project management software. It puts to-dos, message boards, chat, calendars, card tables, files and check-ins in one place for each project.
company.customers: Companies, teams, freelancers and studios that manage projects and work with clients. The plans range from a free personal plan to an Unlimited plan for larger organizations.
company.how_they_sell: Mostly self-serve online. There is a free plan, 30-day or 45-day free trials, and fixed monthly or annual prices with no per-user fees. Personal demos can be booked with the team. Support runs through a web form, around the clock on paid plans, with priority support and personalized onboarding on the top plan. Customers cancel on their own without contacting anyone.
company.size_hints: In business for 27 years, privately held and debt-free. 2,026 organizations signed up in one week. Tens of thousands of companies use the product. More than 200,000 newsletter subscribers.

audit.headline: The first thing worth automating at Basecamp is sorting contact form messages and matching them to accounts, because every pre-sales, support and priority request goes into one hand-sorted queue that the site says is running slower than usual.
audit.caveat: 37signals builds its own tools and often does things by hand on purpose, so the website cannot show what in-house automation already exists or which manual steps the company wants to keep.

signals.observation: Pre-sales questions, help requests and other questions all go through one contact form to the team. Someone has to sort each one by hand.
signals.quote: For pre-sales questions, customers who need a hand, or other inquiries, reach out to our team.

signals.observation: Every message gets a personal reply, and the page warns that replies are slower than usual. This points to a support backlog.
signals.quote: We read and respond to every message, though response times may be a bit longer than usual right now.

signals.observation: The support form asks for an email and account URL typed in by hand. Staff then have to match each request to an account.
signals.quote: This is where we’ll get back to you. Double check that it’s right.

signals.observation: Demos and live Q&A sessions are booked with the team one at a time.
signals.quote: Want a walkthrough? Live Q&A session? Book a personal demo with our team.

signals.observation: Top-plan customers get onboarding walkthroughs from staff. Each one takes staff time.
signals.quote: One of our experts is happy to walk your team through Basecamp to get you up to speed.

signals.observation: Annual billing can be paid by check, ACH or wire. These payments usually need manual matching and reconciliation.
signals.quote: Annual billing by check, ACH, wire, or credit card.

signals.observation: Priority support moves top-plan tickets to the front of a shared queue. That requires sorting tickets by plan.
signals.quote: Jump to the front of the queue when you contact support.

signals.observation: The CEO invites questions by direct email, which adds an inbox that has to be read by hand.
signals.quote: You can always contact me directly if you have any questions at jason@basecamp.com

signals.observation: Support passes customer feedback on new features to the developers who built them, one item at a time.
signals.quote: Be the first port of call for support when they get feedback from customers.

signals.observation: Feedback beyond fixes is logged and weighed against other ideas. This is a manual triage step.
signals.quote: all the feedback that goes beyond that is filed for consideration against all the other ideas and claims for our time.

signals.observation: After each launch, developers watch the error tracker themselves for a while.
signals.quote: Pay attention to the error tracker for a while after launching.

signals.observation: Riskier releases wait for manual exploratory testing by QA, which can hold up shipping.
signals.quote: If you need exploratory testing done by QA to feel confident that your work is solid enough for the criticality at stake

tools.name: Basecamp
tools.quote: So we had to build our own project management system from scratch.

opportunities.title: Sort and account-match contact form messages
opportunities.problem: Pre-sales questions, help requests and other questions all arrive through one form. Staff sort each message by hand, match a typed email and account URL to an account, and pull top-plan tickets to the front, while the page warns that replies are slower than usual.
opportunities.approach: When a form is submitted, look up the email and account URL in the account database and attach the plan, status and account link to the ticket. Rules first, with a language model classifier only if needed, tag each message as pre-sales, support, billing or feedback and send it to the right queue, with top-plan tickets flagged as priority. Mail to the CEO's direct address can be forwarded into the same flow.

measure.metric: Median time from form submit to first human reply, split by category and plan, plus share of messages matched to an account with no staff lookup
measure.baseline: In week 1, pull submit and first-reply timestamps for the last 4 weeks of form messages from the support tool, and time a sample of manual sorts and account lookups
measure.target: Cut median first reply time by at least a third from the measured baseline, and match at least 80% of messages to an account automatically

opportunities.days_30: Baseline measured, account lookup live, plan shown on every ticket.
opportunities.days_60: Category tags and priority routing live, misroutes reviewed weekly with support leads.
opportunities.days_90: CEO inbox folded in, before and after reply times reported to support.
opportunities.assumption: The plan assumes staff sort and match each form message by hand today, when 37signals may already route tickets with its own in-house tools and the slow-reply notice may reflect a short-term staffing gap.
opportunities.ask: When a form message comes in today, what happens before a person reads it, and how much of a support person's time goes to sorting and looking up accounts rather than answering?

opportunities.title: Match check, ACH and wire payments to annual invoices
opportunities.problem: Annual plans can be paid by check, ACH or wire, and these payments usually need someone to match each deposit to an invoice and account by hand. Slow matching can leave paid accounts looking unpaid and delay revenue reporting.
opportunities.approach: Pull bank deposit data each day and match it to open invoices by invoice number, amount and payer name. Clear matches mark the invoice and account as paid, and unclear ones go to a short review list for finance.

measure.metric: Share of non-card payments matched with no manual work, and days from deposit to account marked paid
measure.baseline: In week 1, count last quarter's check, ACH and wire payments from bank and billing records and log how long each took to apply
measure.target: Match most clean payments automatically and apply them within one business day of the deposit

opportunities.days_30: Payment volume and time-to-apply measured, match rules agreed with finance.
opportunities.days_60: Daily matching running alongside the manual process for checking.
opportunities.days_90: Automatic posting live for clean matches, review list for the rest.
opportunities.assumption: The plan assumes enough annual customers pay by check, ACH or wire to make manual matching a real cost, but the site only shows that these payment options exist.
opportunities.ask: How many check, ACH and wire payments do you get each month, and how long does it take to mark one as paid?

opportunities.title: Route feature feedback to the right team and idea log
opportunities.problem: Support passes feedback on new features to the developers who built them one item at a time. Feedback beyond fixes is filed by hand to be weighed later, which takes support time and hides how often the same request comes up.
opportunities.approach: Support tags a ticket with the feature name, and the feedback posts automatically to that feature's Basecamp project with customer and plan attached. Requests that are not fixes go to a shared idea log that groups duplicates and keeps a count.

measure.metric: Time from ticket to feedback showing in the feature's Basecamp project, and support minutes spent forwarding
measure.baseline: In week 1, sample recent forwarded feedback and time each handoff from ticket to developer
measure.target: Feedback reaches the right project within minutes of tagging, with no manual forwarding

opportunities.days_30: Feature tag list agreed with support and product, handoff time measured.
opportunities.days_60: Auto-posting to Basecamp projects live for new features.
opportunities.days_90: Idea log with duplicate counts in use for planning.
opportunities.assumption: The plan assumes forwarding feedback and filing ideas takes real support time, when the handbook may describe a choice to have people read and weigh feedback by hand.
opportunities.ask: How does a piece of feature feedback get from a support ticket to the right developer today, and do you know how often the same request comes up?

dropped.title: Self-serve booking and prep for demos and onboarding
dropped.reason: The plan assumes demos and onboarding calls are frequent and slow to book, when most customers sign up on their own and these calls may be rare.

dropped.title: Alert developers to new errors after each launch
dropped.reason: The plan assumes the error tracker has no alerting today, which is unlikely for a mature engineering team, and the idea would fit almost any software company.

questions: When a form message comes in today, what happens before a person reads it, and how much of a support person's time goes to sorting and looking up accounts rather than answering?
How many check, ACH and wire payments do you get each month, and how long does it take to mark one as paid?
How does a piece of feature feedback get from a support ticket to the right developer today, and do you know how often the same request comes up?
How many people work in support, and how many messages do they handle in a typical week?
Which manual tasks do you want to keep done by people on purpose, and which ones would you gladly hand off?
What tools does support use today to receive, tag and track tickets, and are any of them built in-house?

pages.title: Basecamp — Where we came from
pages.text:
Born out of desperate necessity to stop embarrassing ourselves in front of our clients, the story of how Basecamp was born is likely your story, too.
Hey there, I’m Jason Fried, one of the co-founders here. I’ve been running 37signals — the business that makes Basecamp — for 27 years.
People often ask me why we built Basecamp. They’ve never seen anything like it before, so they’re curious where the idea came from.
I wish I could credit a spark of genius, or some deep insight. But I can’t. Truth is, we built Basecamp out of desperate necessity . We needed it bad. Without it, we were embarrassing ourselves.
Way back when, we used to be a design firm. As we grew, we kept taking on more and more projects. We thought we could handle it, while still providing the same level of service, but we couldn’t. We were fooling ourselves. Sound familiar?
It wasn’t that we didn’t have the skills — we just didn’t have the right tools, nor the method, to juggle the additional workload. We were disorganized, we were dropping balls, and stuff was slipping.
Quality was suffering, and, as is often the case in situations like this, our clients noticed before we noticed. That was the especially painful and uncomfortable part.
We needed a better way to manage projects, track feedback, and make progress. Email, chat, spreadsheets, calls, scattered documents, information here, there, and everywhere just wasn’t cutting it. Systems like that work for a minute, and then they fall apart fast — especially as you grow and add more people to the mix.
We looked around and tried a few things, but the popular tools we tried simply didn’t cut it. So we had to build our own project management system from scratch.
We focused on building a simple, straightforward collection of tools that could track work so everyone knew who was doing what, keep feedback and revisions on the record, centralize communication so no one missed anything, and schedule important milestones.
We started using the system with our clients. They kept asking “What is this? We could totally use this for our own projects!” And that’s when the lightbulb went on — maybe this is a product for others, and not just for us? If we need it, surely others need it.
So we tweaked it, tightened it up, polished the rough edges, and put it on the market. It was an instant hit.
Turns out, tens of thousands of other companies had similar struggles managing their projects, and needed what we needed.
And about a year or so after we first released it, it was generating more revenue for us than our web design business. So we stopped doing web design and have been focused on building Basecamp ever since.
Based on feedback, and our own ideas, we’ve made thousands of improvements over the years, with so much more to come. Basecamp defined a category, and continues to constantly push that category forward in innovative ways.
It’s been an incredible ride so far, and we have so many people to thank. But most of all, we feel a deep sense of responsibility to continue to make the best product we can for companies who desperately seek a better way to work. We’re here for them, 23 years and running.
Thanks for reading, and for giving Basecamp a try . You can always contact me directly if you have any questions at jason@basecamp.com . I look forward to hearing from you.
Jason Fried, jason@basecamp.com
Co-founder & CEO

pages.title: Basecamp — Features, benefits, benefits, and benefits
pages.text:
Where there’s work, there’s Basecamp
If there are tasks to do, discussions to have, decisions to make, files to share, deadlines to hit, relationships to manage, and work to deliver, Basecamp helps make it happen. Here’s just some of what Basecamp can do for you.
The Project page keeps it all together
Every project in Basecamp gets its own page. Add the tools you need (to-dos, message boards, chat, a calendar, card tables), then invite co-workers, clients, even AI Agents. Everything stays organized, automatically.
Message Boards for announcements and discussions
Message Boards replace email. Announcements and discussions live as posts, with every reply attached right below. It’s all in one place, so even people you bring in later can get up to speed quickly.
To-do Lists for tracking all the little things
Make a list, or ten lists. Assign items, set due dates, attach files, even create subtasks. It’s all so simple when it’s in Basecamp for your entire team to see.
Hill Charts show you where things really stand
Is the project going to be done on time? Are people stuck? Basecamp’s Hill Charts let you know exactly where things really stand. Interesting, tell me more .
Card Tables for tracking work through stages
Card Tables are our take on kanban boards. Add cards, set up columns, and move work through phases. Perfect for bug and issue tracking, software development, production work, or anything with distinct stages.
Campfire chats for quick, casual conversations
With Basecamp you don’t need Slack, WhatsApp, or another chat app. Just chat in Basecamp instead. Perfect for real-time conversations, quick file sharing, random questions, stuff like that.
The Basecamp Calendar for big dates
Add a built-in calendar to your project for deadlines, milestones, events, and meetings. A global calendar brings every project together, and you can subscribe in Outlook, Google Calendar, HEY Calendar, and more.
Automatic Check-ins for recurring questions
Cut back on meetings by setting up Automatic Check-ins. Basecamp asks your team questions on a schedule, like “What are you working on this week?” every Monday at 9am, and saves everyone’s answers in one place.
Docs & Files for reference materials, assets, and links
Docs & Files keeps images, documents, PDFs, even cloud files from Figma, Google Docs, and Dropbox neatly organized inside your projects. Brand assets, approved designs, all in one spot everyone can find.
My Tasks, Events, Today, Bookmarks, and Notes
Get instant access to your tasks, events, bookmarks, and notes, right from the “My Bar” at the bottom of the screen. It’s keyboard accessible too, so you can pop your assignments up without touching the mouse.
Reports for high-level overviews
Get an instant read on where things stand with Basecamp’s Reports.
Everything Views are like having x-ray vision
A real game changer, Everything Views pull everything of one type onto a single page, no matter which project it’s in. Know someone uploaded a file but don’t remember where? Check “All Files” and it’ll be right there.
The Lineup is your bird’s eye view
Want to see every project plotted on a timeline based on start and end dates? Then you want The Lineup. See overlaps, see beginnings and ends, see who’s on what, even see key dates superimposed over everything. You’ll love it.
API, CLI, SDK, Skills, and Integrations
Connect other services with the Basecamp API , add 3rd party integrations , work from the command line (CLI) , or invite your favorite AI agent . Claude, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor — all are welcome.
Keyboard shortcuts speed everything up
Hit SHIFT and little keys appear next to everything you can navigate to. Add that letter to jump right there, no mouse required.
Decide what clients get to see
Working with a client? Basecamp’s Client mode lets you decide what they should — and shouldn’t — see, project by project. Hide unfinished work, keep conversations on the record, and collaborate together. It’s a win-win.
Activity that’s easy to absorb
In Basecamp, activity is neatly organized by topic, clearly attributed, and time-stamped. Scroll back to see what happened yesterday, last week, or since the beginning of time. Quiet stretches show too.

pages.title: Basecamp — Seven Shipping Principles
pages.text:
Seven Shipping Principles
Core fundamentals that inform how we go about building — and shipping — great software at a sustainable pace.
We only ship good work
This might sound self-evident, but in reality there are all sorts of pressures that might lead you to ship mediocre or even iffy work. We promised the feature! We spent a lot of time on it! It’s not horrible ! From the user’s perspective, it’s actually sorta fine?
None of these excuses are adequate reasons for us to ship anything but good work at 37signals. This means solid implementations in terms of design and programming, CSS and JavaScript, Ruby and operations. Work we’d be pleased to have to revisit 9 months later without a sigh of dread.
Most things we work on at 37signals will be around until the end of the internet . So whatever short-term gain you can capture by shipping short of good, you’ll lose when you have to work on it again later (and eventually you will!).
This isn’t just about productivity, now or in the future, but also about pride in the work. The delight that comes from working with code and design that’s properly built. It’s hard to put a specific price on that, but easy to recognize the smile it puts on your face.
This is not a general license to gold-plate everything. We intentionally constrain ourselves through the cycles in Shape Up , such that we don’t end up spending 2 months on stuff that warranted 2 weeks worth of work. Not every batch of work is going to be a 10/10. But if it’s less than 8/10, it probably shouldn’t go out the door. If it’s less than a 7/10, there’s no way it should go out the door, except as an emergency patch you immediately return to cleanup.
Shipping good work takes discipline and sacrifice. We will afford ourselves both.
We ship when we’re confident
The reason we do automated and exploratory testing is so we can ship work with confidence that it won’t cause major problems. But exactly how much confidence is required depends both on the team and the criticality of the problem. It’s a measure to gauge in relation to the specifics of the work, not mindlessly delegate to a standardized process.
If you’re working on a small change that’s of low criticality, you don’t need the same due diligence as if you’re working on a big change of high criticality. That might seem obvious, but it’s easy just to run the familiar process, and forget to check whether it makes sense for the particulars.
High criticality work involves anything that mutates or munges data. If you can lose data, it’s high criticality. It also involves anything that makes larger changes to existing and big features. If you’re rewriting how todos in Basecamp work, you better be pretty sure you’ve checked everything twice or thrice. If a bug makes it to production on high criticality work, it’s a big deal.
Lower criticality work is anything that merely changes the presentation of existing data, or works on entirely new sets of data, or deals with screens or features off the critical path. If a bug makes it to production on lower criticality work, it won’t be a big deal. You fix it and move on.
It’s up to the team to gauge whether what they’re working on is high or lower criticality or somewhere in-between. It also depends on who works on it. Someone well-versed in the domain? A lead with 10 years of experience? They’ll deem more things lower criticality than someone who just started recently. This is natural and right.
If you need exploratory testing done by QA to feel confident that your work is solid enough for the criticality at stake, that’s what you should do. Even if it means waiting a bit to be able to ship. But if you’re confident that the work is likely to be good enough for the criticality at stake, you should just ship, stick around to deal with issues, and keep moving forward.
You gauge your confidence, and if in doubt, check with someone more senior. The process, the tools, and the testing are there to increase your confidence. Not to tell you when it’s time to ship or not.
We ship when the work is finished
It’s rare here to keep work that’s essentially finished behind a feature flag for long if at all. We don’t start a lot of highly speculative projects. If it’s been kicked off, it’s because we’ve decided we need it, and that means it’s going out the kitchen when it’s cooked.
This means we’re not sitting on a large inventory of possibly-maybe projects that linger behind a feature flag until something magical happens. We clear the decks so we can get on with new work.
That runs the risk that we’ll occasionally ship a project that isn’t quite right once we see it in the wild. That’s okay. If it’s bad enough, we’ll fix it then. We don’t have billions of users. They won’t die or leave in droves just because we launch something that perhaps could have been better if it had been done a different way from the start.
The momentum of shipping good work has a quality all of its own. We don’t halt the momentum unless it’s properly bad, we don’t linger around second-guessing ourselves ad nauseam. The show must go on.
We own the issues after we ship
Clean up your own mess if you make one. Pay attention to the error tracker for a while after launching. Be the first port of call for support when they get feedback from customers. If you did the work, you have the context, and you should put it straight if it’s crooked.
This sometimes means that you will have started something new and then get pulled away to fix something old. If it’s a substantial issue, that’s just what it is. You put the new on hold while you fix the old.
But you also have to keep the line on what “substantial” means. Almost everything we ship is met with a range of feedback. People will want more or less or different or better or whatever no matter how perfect the work. You can spend an eternity refining and reworking even the smallest change if you let yourself. We don’t let ourselves.
So you’re on the hook to make it right, to make it work as intended, but all the feedback that goes beyond that is filed for consideration against all the other ideas and claims for our time.
Ship it, fix it, forget it.
We don’t ship if it isn’t right
It can be frustrating when work is held in the 11th hour because an issue or an insight that just popped up gives us pause. Why didn’t you mention this three weeks ago? Yes, it’s indeed better to get feedback early, but often that’s just not possible, because the issue or the insight isn’t apparent until it’s go time.

pages.title: Basecamp — Books we’ve written
pages.text:
On top of making Basecamp, we write books about what we’ve learned running our own business. They’re filled with practical advice you won’t find anywhere else.
Shape Up is for product development teams who struggle to ship. Written by the innovators behind Basecamp — one of the biggest and longest-running software as a service apps — the book gives teams the tools to address the risks and unknowns at each stage of the product development process. Full of eye-opening insights, Shape Up will help you break free of “best practices” that aren’t really working, think deeper about the right problems, and start shipping meaningful projects your team can celebrate.
Buy the print edition
Read it online
Download a PDF
It Doesn’t Have to Be Crazy at Work
Chaos shouldn’t be the natural state at work. Anxiety isn’t a prerequisite for progress. Sitting in meetings all day isn’t required for success. These are all perversions of work — side effects of broken models and “best” practices. This book treats the patient, calls out false cures, and pushes back against ritualistic time-sucks that have infected the way people work these days.

New York Times bestseller! Most business books give you the same old advice: write a business plan, study the competition, seek investors, yadda yadda.
